concepts.name: Responsive Desire
concepts.definition: Sexual interest that arises in response to stimulation or erotic context, rather than appearing spontaneously beforehand.
concepts.summary: Desire can arrive after touch, context, or connection begins. That pattern is common and valid.

blocks.title: Recognize
blocks.body: Do you rarely feel random urges for sex, but once things start, you get into it and enjoy yourself?

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.body: Desire research describes responsive desire as a common, healthy pattern, especially for women and in long-term relationships. Lack of spontaneous urge beforehand does not mean low libido; many people become interested once touch, mood, or connection engages them.

blocks.title: Field Note
blocks.body: What conditions help you become curious after you begin: comfort, pacing, emotional closeness, type of touch, or something else?

blocks.title: A Phrase To Keep
blocks.body: I do not always feel desire before we begin, but sometimes it shows up once there is warmth, touch, and no pressure.

phraseTemplates.label: For myself
phraseTemplates.body: I am learning that responsive desire may matter for me, and I want to notice it without turning it into a goal.

phraseTemplates.label: Ask for support
phraseTemplates.body: Can we make space for making room for responsive desire slowly, with check-ins about what feels good and what does not?

phraseTemplates.label: Set a boundary
phraseTemplates.body: If responsive desire starts to feel pressured or uncomfortable, I want us to pause and choose a different pace.

phraseTemplates.label: Open curiosity
phraseTemplates.body: I am curious about making room for responsive desire, and I would like to treat it as an experiment rather than something we have to get right.

phraseTemplates.label: Reassure
phraseTemplates.body: Nothing is wrong if responsive desire shows up differently from one experience to the next. I want patience and honesty to lead.

concepts.name: Angling
concepts.definition: Rotating, raising, or lowering the pelvis during penetration to adjust where internal stimulation occurs.
concepts.summary: Small changes in pelvic angle can redirect pressure and make a familiar position feel different.

blocks.title: Recognize
blocks.body: Have you ever shifted your hips during penetration to find an angle that felt better?

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.body: The OMGyes Pleasure Report identified angling as a named technique associated with enhanced pleasure. Naming the movement can help you notice it in the moment and repeat what works instead of relying on a vague memory of a position.

blocks.title: Field Note
blocks.body: What angle, height, or position tends to make internal pressure feel more focused for you?

blocks.title: A Phrase To Keep
blocks.body: A small change in angle can make a big difference for me. I may want to slow down and adjust my hips until the pressure lands right.

concepts.name: Pairing
concepts.definition: Adding external clitoral stimulation during penetration, either solo or with a partner.
concepts.summary: Penetration and external clitoral touch can work together rather than competing for attention.

blocks.title: Recognize
blocks.body: Have you found that penetration alone does not quite get you there, but adding clitoral touch changes everything?

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.body: Research consistently links clitoral stimulation with higher orgasm likelihood during partnered sex. Pairing treats external touch as common, useful information about anatomy, not as a fix for something wrong.

blocks.title: Field Note
blocks.body: What kind of external touch, pressure, rhythm, or tool tends to pair well with internal sensation for you?

blocks.title: A Phrase To Keep
blocks.body: Penetration feels better for me when it is paired with clitoral touch. I would like that to be part of the experience, not an extra.

concepts.name: Spectatoring
concepts.definition: Mentally watching and evaluating yourself during sex rather than staying present in the experience.
concepts.summary: Self-monitoring can pull attention away from sensation and into performance commentary.

blocks.title: Recognize
blocks.body: Have you caught yourself thinking about how you look, whether you are taking too long, or what your partner might be thinking?

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.body: Masters and Johnson named spectatoring as a barrier to enjoyment. Later research links self-focused attention during sex with lower arousal and satisfaction, while mindfulness-based approaches can help redirect attention back to sensation.

blocks.title: Field Note
blocks.body: What kind of thoughts tend to pull you out of your body? What sensory cue could help you come back?

blocks.title: A Phrase To Keep
blocks.body: Sometimes I get in my head and start monitoring myself. Slowing down and focusing on sensation helps me come back.

concepts.name: Non-concordance
concepts.definition: When physical arousal signs do not match the subjective feeling of being turned on, and vice versa.
concepts.summary: Genital response and felt desire can diverge. Wanting is communicated, not inferred from physical signs.

blocks.title: Recognize
blocks.body: Have you ever felt mentally aroused while your body showed few signs, or noticed physical response when you were not actually interested?

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.body: Meta-analyses find only modest correlation between genital response and subjective arousal in women. Genital response can occur without desire, and desire can exist without obvious physical signs. Consent and wanting are communicated, not inferred.

blocks.title: Field Note
blocks.body: Where have you noticed a mismatch between body signals and felt wanting? What would help you trust your own experience?

blocks.title: A Phrase To Keep
blocks.body: My body signals and my felt desire are not always the same thing. I want us to listen to what I say I want, not guess from physical signs.
